answer:
Filtering changes what the assistant read; it cannot change what the caller may do. Authorization is a relation between an authenticated principal, a specific action and a specific object, decided against policy - not a property of text. The principal table lists a retrieved document as untrusted data, not executable instruction or approval to call another tool, so neither the sentence's presence nor its removal confers authority.

Filtering is also unsound as a gate: there is "no foolproof natural-language filter", and the risk is structural once retrieved text is merged into high-priority instructions or read as a tool command. Paraphrase, encoding, citations and titles evade any text check, so filtering is depth in defense, never enforcement.

The check belongs at the authority that protects the effect: a separate action API whose server-side enforcement point evaluates subject-action-resource entitlement, validates arguments against a narrow schema and allowed IDs, and rechecks entitlement "even if the agent previously searched successfully". Deny by default, re-evaluate at execution including delayed jobs, fail closed when authority cannot be established. Human confirmation suits irreversible effects but is not a substitute for ACLs; model confidence never replaces deterministic checks.

Evidence map: principal-tools sections 1-3; security-architecture section 2; decision gates section 7.

evidence.claim: A retrieved document is untrusted data and is explicitly not executable instruction or approval to call another tool.
evidence.note: Observed: principal table gives retrieved document/search result the control 'Untrusted data, source ID, revision and access classification' and the 'It is not' cell 'Executable instruction or approval to call another tool'; the action executor holds 'Independent permission enforcement', not authority delegated because a model requested it. Same section states every read and every action is evaluated against the actual authorized subject and object, citing deny-by-default least privilege.

evidence.claim: Any separately allowed action must pass its own authorization, schema, risk and confirmation gate rather than inherit authority from a retrieved paragraph.
evidence.note: Observed: text alternative to the flow diagram says 'Any separately allowed action must pass its own authorization, schema, risk and confirmation gate - not inherit authority from a retrieved paragraph.' The diagram separates a 'Bounded data result (untrusted content)' into a reasoning client that may only call a 'Separate action API' behind a 'Policy / confirmation / effect gate'. Also: 'A model's confidence or chain-of-thought is never a replacement for deterministic access checks.'

evidence.claim: Text filtering cannot be a sound authorization gate because no foolproof natural-language filter exists and the failure mode is structural.
evidence.note: Observed: 'There is **no foolproof natural-language filter**; preventing unacceptable effects requires server-side boundaries that do not depend solely on how the language model interprets prose.' Also 'A guard based only on "ignore malicious text" is fragile: the risk is structural when retrieved text is merged into high-priority instructions or interpreted as a tool command.' Controls listed include provenance labelling, capability limits, narrow argument schemas, and independent confirmation.

evidence.claim: Entitlement must be checked again at the authority that protects the effect, even after a successful search, and confirmation does not replace ACLs.
evidence.note: Observed: 'Check entitlement **again at the authority that protects the effect**, even if the agent previously searched successfully.' and 'Require explicit independent human confirmation for actions with significant irreversible impact where appropriate; confirmation is not a substitute for ACLs.' This is the location answer: the effect-protecting authority, not the retrieval layer or the prompt.

evidence.claim: Enforcement is a reproducible subject-resource-action policy decision at a named enforcement point, re-decided when delayed work executes.
evidence.note: Observed: the service/API handler 'authorizes subject-resource-action pairs with authenticated context and explicit tenant ownership'; the asynchronous path binds intent at enqueue time 'then performs a new validity/replay/expiry decision when execution occurs. A delayed job is not automatically authorized forever'; a policy decision must record 'policy revision, identity assurance, resource ownership snapshot, action, expiry, reason code, enforcement point and outcome'.

evidence.claim: Deny by default, test confused-deputy paths, and fail closed when authority cannot be established.
evidence.note: Observed: 'Network location is not trust; a valid token is not object permission.' Failure guidance: 'Deny by default, test indirect and confused-deputy paths, keep a bounded break-glass path with audit, and fail closed when authority cannot be established.'

evidence.claim: The agent is an untrusted proposer; a separate authority records the affirmative decision, so model self-assessment never becomes authorization.
evidence.note: Observed: 'treat an autonomous coding agent as an *untrusted proposer* of bounded diffs'; 'A separate reviewer validates the dangerous boundaries and records an affirmative decision; no other agent's self-assessment can be silently promoted to independent human acceptance.' Inference: this is written for code-change agents; I extend the same separation to general tool calls.

confidence: high for the mechanism; the cited pages are conceptual and carry evidence_status unknown, content_review self-checked, with no runtime or production measurement.
unknowns: No section addressing classifier or guardrail evasion specifically was found; the dedicated-evasion gap is inferred from the 'no foolproof natural-language filter' statement rather than measured.
Atlas and modeling-and-simulation layers were not reachable through the documented CLI surface (search accepts no layer or volume flag), so cross-layer coverage of this question is unverified.
The book gives no threshold for when human confirmation is required, only 'significant irreversible impact where appropriate'.
